sources.citation: Agostiniani, Luciano. 2006. "Epigrafia e lingua elime: un bilancio". In Guerra e pace in Sicilia e nel Mediterraneo antico (VIII-III sec. a.C.). Arte, prassi e teoria della pace e della guerra. Atti delle quinte giornate internazionali di studi sull'area elima e la Sicilia occidentale nel contesto mediterraneo (Erice, 12-15 ottobre 2003), vol. II, 683-688. Pisa: Edizioni della Normale.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing on accent. Content: Elymian is IE and flexional; Ambrosini/Georgiev Anatolian theses rejected; Lejeune's Italic thesis rests on saritu-/peiie-; 'points of no return': Selinuntine alphabet with reversed-N = /b/, ordinary beta = a labial fricative /f/ or /phi/; nominatives in -a, datives in -ai with emi ('atai tukai emi'), coin legend Segestazib emi = dat. pl. < *-bhi; refutation of Marchesini 1998 (reversed-N as mis-executed ny); the -a + emi formula in new graffiti (*382, *385) read as nominative or as a Greek genitive on a local name.

sources.note: No rule or statement of word accent. The only accent-adjacent words found anywhere in the Elymian literature opened: arguing against the apocope of final -i in -b < *-bhi, Biondi notes that final -i is preserved 'in emi (sebbene qui presumibilmente essa sia tonica)' -- a parenthetical assumption that the final vowel of the one verb form emi 'I am' carries the accent (page image checked); footnote 18 concerns the Erycine spelling -aziib, not accent. Rest of the paper: morphology of -a / -a(a)i / -azib (read as genitives), formulae of possession, coin legends.

sources.note: Phonology content is limited to segmental/comparative remarks (p.241-242): Elymian is Indo-European (emi 'je suis'), 'une langue centum (occlusives p, t, k; b, d, g) à cinq timbres vocaliques (c'est-à-dire sans confusions de o et a)', with conservation of initial *s- (and probably *y-) before vowel; script is dextroverse Greek alphabet without word separation. Nothing on accent, stress or quantity; the corpus (abbreviated names, datives in -ai/-oi/-ei, a few verb forms) carries no accent notation.
